source.anchor_kjv: For the bodies of those beasts, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate. Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
source.hook_line: The man who would carry the cross of Jesus was walking the other way.
source.spoken_script: The man who would carry the cross of Jesus was walking the other way. Mark says the soldiers "led him out to crucify him. And they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country." Jesus, out of the city. Simon, in from the country. Same road. They put the cross on Simon's back. Nobody asked him. Luke says, "on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." Simon turns, and walks out too. Now he is through the gate. In the King James Bible, outside is "without." The sin offering, an animal killed for the people's sin, had its blood carried into the sanctuary, God's holy tent. Its body went out, burned "without the camp." Then it says of Jesus: "Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate." Out there, where Simon is walking. Hebrews turns to you: "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach." Reproach is shame. Bearing it is carrying it, as Simon carried the wood. Simon was forced out. You are asked. Turn on your own road, and carry his shame after him, freely this time. Only the shame. He went out through that gate first, and the atoning, the dying, the finishing, that was his, with his own blood.

platforms.title: The Man Who Carried Jesus' Cross Was Walking the Other Way
platforms.description:
Hebrews 13 says Jesus "suffered without the gate." But the first man to walk outside that gate carrying a cross wasn't Jesus.

Mark says the soldiers "compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country." The cross meant for Jesus went onto Simon's own shoulders. Nobody asked him.

Then Hebrews turns the same invitation toward us: "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

Simon carried it forced. We're only asked to carry the shame, freely this time. The atoning was His alone, with His own blood.

platforms.title: Simon of Cyrene: Forced to Carry Jesus' Cross (Mark 15, Hebrews 13)
platforms.description:
Simon of Cyrene wasn't walking toward Jesus that morning. Mark 15 says he was "coming out of the country," heading the opposite way, when Roman soldiers "compel" him to carry the cross meant for someone else. Nobody asked him. Luke adds the detail: "on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." Simon turns, and follows.

Then Hebrews reaches back to the sin offering, the animal whose blood went into the sanctuary, but whose body was burned "without the camp," and lands it on Jesus Himself: "Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate." Out there, on the same ground Simon was forced to walk.

And Hebrews doesn't stop at history. It turns to you: "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach." Reproach is shame. Bearing it is carrying it, the way Simon carried the wood.

Simon was forced out. You are only asked. The atoning, the dying, the finishing, that was His, with His own blood. All that's left for us to carry is the shame, and this time, freely.
